en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Twentieth Chapter
The Discourse on Knowledge:
Is it the case that an ordinary person lacks knowledge?
Yes, it is.
“Is there no wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena, discernment, close discernment, and precise discernment in an ordinary person?
“One should not say so.
“… Is it not the case that there is wisdom, understanding, investigation, and so forth, in an ordinary person?”
Is it a characteristic of discernment? Yes.
If so, does an ordinary person possess wisdom, understanding, investigation, and so forth? Yes.
[This is] a specific discernment; indeed, it should not be said that "there is no knowledge for the worldling.
Is there no knowledge for the worldling?
“Yes.
“Then does an ordinary person (puthujjana) enter the first jhāna?
“Yes.”
If an ordinary person were to attain the first jhāna, then indeed it should not be said:
"An ordinary person has no knowledge.
[The same applies if] an ordinary person were to attain the second jhāna... [and so on].
...the third jhāna ...
the fourth jhāna ...
he might attain the base of infinite space.
One might attain the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
or a worldling might give a gift … [and so on] … might give a robe.
"Would one give almsfood,
would one give lodging,
or would one give medicinal requisites for the sick?"
“Yes.
“If an ordinary person were to give medicinal requisites for the sick, surely it should not be said:
‘An ordinary person has no knowledge.’”
Is there knowledge belonging to an ordinary person (puthujjana)? Yes.
Does that ordinary person, by means of that knowledge, fully understand suffering, abandon its origin, realize its cessation, and develop the path?
It should not be stated thus... [etc.
...The Discussion on Knowledge is finished.
